name: dns2tcp
why: Tunnels TCP through DNS queries, a vivid door into how DNS can carry arbitrary traffic past firewalls.

brief.what_it_is: dns2tcp is a set of command-line tools that tunnels a TCP session inside DNS packets. Per the Debian package description, it encapsulates TCP in DNS queries and replies, and the client does not need root privileges. The brew metadata lists two executables, dns2tcpc (client) and dns2tcpd (server). I did not read the upstream README, so details on exactly what goes in and out are not confirmed.
brief.why_it_exists: The Debian description frames it as a way to carry a TCP session over DNS, claiming this produces smaller packets than IP-over-DNS and so improves throughput. The motivation to get past restrictive networks is the scout note's framing, not something I confirmed in the package text.
brief.how_it_works: The Debian description says only that it encapsulates a TCP session in DNS packets, and that this yields smaller packets than IP-over-DNS. I did not find a mechanism explanation in the pages I read.
brief.install_notes: Installable via Debian packages (dns2tcp 0.5.2-4 in sid, with builds for many architectures) and, per the brew metadata, via Homebrew. The Debian dependencies are only init-system-helpers and libc6. I saw no first-run or configuration steps, since the upstream README was not read.
brief.standout: Tunnelling TCP over DNS queries, rather than IP-over-DNS, is the notable choice, and the Debian text claims it gives smaller packets and better throughput. The client running without root is also worth noting.
brief.status: Packaged and maintained in Debian: the package page shows version 0.5.2-4 in sid with two named maintainers and builds for many architectures. I found no upstream release date or last-commit date, so upstream activity is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a Debian package listing, not the project's own site, and it gives no usage docs. The upstream page I tried (hsc.fr) returned an unrelated French security article, so I could not confirm the upstream project or its README. The brief rests on the Debian description alone, and no commands were verified.

entry.title: dns2tcp
entry.tldr: A client and server pair that wrap a TCP session inside DNS queries and replies, showing how a name lookup can carry arbitrary traffic.
entry.deeper_look:
dns2tcp is a set of tools that encapsulate a TCP session in DNS packets. Homebrew installs two executables: `dns2tcpc`, the client, and `dns2tcpd`, the server. The Debian description notes that the client does not need root privileges.

The design choice the package text highlights is carrying TCP directly, rather than tunnelling whole IP packets over DNS. In its words, "This type of encapsulation generates smaller packets than IP-over-DNS, improving throughput." The brief does not explain the mechanism in more detail, so how data is packed into queries and replies is something to find out by reading the source or running it.

The idea underneath is that DNS is a protocol almost every network lets through, and that its queries and answers are just structured bytes that can hold something else. Poking at a tunnel like this is a good way to learn what DNS messages look like on the wire and why a resolver chain can end up relaying traffic it was never meant to. The usual motivation is getting past restrictive networks, though the package text does not say so directly.

The homepage listed is a Debian package page with no usage docs, so expect to work from the man pages and source after install.

entry.whats_unique: It tunnels a TCP session directly instead of full IP-over-DNS, which the Debian description says gives smaller packets and better throughput. The client runs without root.
entry.caveats: The only source behind this entry is the Debian package description; no usage docs were found, the upstream site could not be confirmed, and upstream activity is unknown.
